title: Women Build Stronger Workplace Friendships, Study Says
paragraphs: Friendships at work can make a job more enjoyable. But according to a new study, men and women tend to make friends at work in quite different ways.

The study was led by Andrew Parker, a professor of leadership at Durham University Business School in the UK, together with researchers from the US and Switzerland. It was published in August in the journal Social Networks.
The researchers followed about 150 employees during their first ten months at a new organization. During that time, the employees completed four surveys about the friendships they had formed at work.

The study found that women were more likely to make new friends through people they already knew. In other words, they often became friends with a friend of a friend. As a result, women built larger workplace networks, in which many of their friends were also connected to each other. These friendships were also more often with other women.

Men, on the other hand, tended to be more selective. They were more likely to form one-to-one friendships and less likely to make friends through mutual contacts. Their friendships were more often with other men, and they were especially common when a friendship seemed to help with personal or career goals.
According to the researchers, women's friendship networks helped to make organizations more stable, while men's friendships seemed to focus more on individual benefits.

The researchers also suggested that these differences could affect equality at work, including the gender pay gap. Women's networks may give them fewer connections to powerful people who can help their careers, while men's more strategic friendships may bring them more professional advantages.

Previous research has shown that close relationships at work are linked to higher engagement, productivity and innovation. For this reason, the researchers recommend that companies create more chances for employees to connect with people across the whole organization.
